title: UNIT 4: DYNAMICS
notes: ✓ Dynamics → Studies the relationship between forces and the motion of objects.

title: 4.1 THE CONCEPT OF FORCE AND NEWTON’S LAWS OF MOTION
notes:
✓ Force → An interaction that can change an object's motion or produce deformation.

✓ Force → A vector quantity measured in newtons (N).

◆ TYPES OF FORCES
✓ Contact forces → Require physical contact, e.g. friction, normal force and tension.

✓ Field forces → Act without direct contact, e.g. gravitational, electric and magnetic forces.

◆ FOUR FUNDAMENTAL FORCES
Gravitational force
Electromagnetic force
Strong nuclear force
Weak nuclear force

◆ COMMON FORCES
✓ Weight → Gravitational force on a body:
W = mg

✓ Normal force → Contact force perpendicular to a surface.

✓ Tension → Pulling force transmitted through a string, rope or cable.

◆ INCLINED PLANE
✓ For a body on an incline of angle θ:

✓ Component of weight parallel to plane → mg sinθ

✓ Component perpendicular to plane → mg cosθ

✓ Normal force → FN = mg cosθ when no other perpendicular force acts.

◆ NEWTON’S FIRST LAW — LAW OF INERTIA
✓ An object remains at rest or continues with constant velocity in a straight line unless acted on by an unbalanced external force.

✓ Inertia → Tendency of a body to resist changes in its state of motion.

✓ Mass → Measures the inertia of an object.

◆ APPLICATIONS
✓ Seat belts and airbags → Reduce injuries by dealing with the effects of inertia during sudden changes in motion.

◆ NEWTON’S SECOND LAW
✓ The acceleration of an object depends directly on the net force and inversely on its mass:

Fnet = ma

a = Fnet/m

✓ Greater net force → Greater acceleration.
✓ Greater mass → Smaller acceleration for the same force.

◆ NEWTON’S THIRD LAW
✓ For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

FAB = −FBA

✓ Action–reaction forces → Act on different bodies, so they do not cancel each other on one body.

◆ IMPORTANT APPLICATIONS
Objects connected by strings
Multiple blocks
Inclined planes
Elevators and tension
Atwood’s machine
Systems involving friction

✓ Elevator accelerating upward:
T = m(g + a)

✓ Elevator accelerating downward:
T = m(g − a)

◆ FREE-BODY DIAGRAM (FBD)
✓ Free-body diagram → Represents only the forces acting directly on the chosen object.

✓ Arrows → Show force direction and may represent relative magnitude.

✓ Use FBD → Resolve forces into components → Apply ΣF = ma.

title: 4.2 FRICTIONAL FORCE
notes:
✓ Friction → A force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between contacting surfaces.

◆ TYPES OF FRICTION
✓ Static friction → Acts between surfaces that are not sliding relative to each other.

✓ Kinetic friction → Acts while one surface slides over another.

✓ Rolling friction → Resistance associated with rolling motion.

✓ Fluid friction → Resistance experienced when an object moves through a fluid.

◆ STATIC FRICTION
✓ Static friction adjusts itself to prevent slipping:
Fs ≤ μsFN

✓ Maximum static friction:
Fs,max = μsFN

◆ KINETIC FRICTION
✓ Once surfaces slide:
Fk = μkFN

✓ Usually μs > μk → It generally requires more force to start an object moving than to keep it sliding.

◆ COEFFICIENT OF FRICTION
✓ μ = Frictional force / Normal force

✓ It is dimensionless and depends on the contacting surfaces.

◆ FRICTION ON AN INCLINE
✓ For a block sliding down an incline:

Fparallel = mg sinθ

FN = mg cosθ

Fk = μkmg cosθ

✓ When sliding downward:
a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ)

◆ CRITICAL ANGLE
✓ At the limiting condition for slipping:
μs = tanθc

✓ Therefore:
θc = tan⁻¹(μs)

◆ USES & EFFECTS
Friction is useful for walking, braking, gripping and transmitting motion.

Friction can also cause energy loss, heating and wear.

✓ Key idea → Friction does not simply mean 'opposite to motion'; it opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces.

title: 4.3 THE FIRST CONDITION OF EQUILIBRIUM
notes:
✓ Equilibrium → The state in which an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity because the resultant force is zero.

◆ FIRST CONDITION OF EQUILIBRIUM
✓ ΣF = 0

✓ For two-dimensional problems:
ΣFx = 0
ΣFy = 0

✓ Forces may act on an object → Their vector sum is zero.

◆ EQUILIBRIUM TYPES
✓ Static equilibrium → Object is at rest.

✓ Dynamic equilibrium → Object moves with constant velocity.

◆ FORCE COMPONENTS
✓ Resolve angled forces into horizontal and vertical components → Apply:
ΣFx = 0
ΣFy = 0

◆ APPLICATIONS
Suspended objects
Traffic lights and cables
Objects on surfaces
Tension problems
Balanced forces

✓ Being at rest → Does not mean that no forces act on an object.

✓ Being at rest → Means the forces balance so that the net force is zero.

title: 4.4 WORK, ENERGY AND POWER
notes:
✓ Work → Describes energy transferred when a force causes displacement.

◆ WORK DONE BY A CONSTANT FORCE
✓ W = Fs cosθ

✓ F → Force
✓ s → Displacement
✓ θ → Angle between force and displacement.

◆ SIGN OF WORK
✓ Positive work → Force has a component in the direction of displacement.

✓ Negative work → Force has a component opposite to displacement.

✓ Zero work → Force is perpendicular to displacement or displacement is zero.

✓ Maximum positive work → Occurs when θ = 0°.

✓ For a varying force → Work is obtained from the area under the force–displacement (F–s) graph.

◆ NET WORK
✓ Wnet = Fnet s

◆ WORK–ENERGY THEOREM
✓ Net work done on an object → Equals its change in kinetic energy:
Wnet = ΔKE = KEf − KEi

◆ KINETIC ENERGY
✓ Energy due to motion:
KE = ½mv²

✓ Kinetic energy → Is always non-negative.

◆ GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY
✓ Near Earth's surface:
PEg = mgh

✓ Only the change in height matters:
ΔPEg = mgΔh

◆ ELASTIC POTENTIAL ENERGY
✓ Energy stored in a stretched or compressed spring:
PEe = ½kx²

✓ k → Spring constant
✓ x → Extension/compression

◆ CONSERVATIVE & NON-CONSERVATIVE FORCES
✓ Conservative force → Work between two points is independent of path; work over a closed path is zero.

✓ Examples → Gravitational force and spring force.

✓ Non-conservative force → Work depends on the path.

✓ Example → Friction.

◆ POWER
✓ Power → Rate at which work is done or energy is transferred:
P = W/t

✓ For constant force and velocity in the force direction:
P = Fv

✓ Unit → Watt (W).

✓ Key idea → Work transfers energy; kinetic and potential energies describe moving and stored forms of mechanical energy; power tells how quickly energy is transferred.

title: 4.5 CONSERVATION OF MECHANICAL ENERGY
notes:
✓ Mechanical energy → The sum of kinetic and potential energies:
ME = KE + PE

✓ For a system with no dissipative forces:
ΔME = 0

✓ Therefore:
KEi + PEi = KEf + PEf

◆ ENERGY TRANSFORMATIONS
✓ Falling object → Gravitational PE decreases while KE increases.

✓ Object moving upward → KE decreases while gravitational PE increases.

✓ Spring → Elastic PE can transform into KE.

◆ WITH FRICTION
✓ Friction → Is a non-conservative force, so mechanical energy is not conserved by itself.

✓ Some mechanical energy → Is transformed into thermal/internal energy.

✓ Work done by friction → Can be related to the change in mechanical energy:
Wf = ΔME

✓ For kinetic and potential energy:
Wf = ΔKE + ΔPE

◆ COMMON ENERGY FORMS
✓ KE = ½mv²

✓ Gravitational PE = mgh

✓ Elastic PE = ½kx²

✓ Key idea → In an ideal system, mechanical energy changes form but the total mechanical energy remains constant. With friction, mechanical energy decreases while total energy is still conserved.

title: 4.6 IMPULSE AND LINEAR MOMENTUM
notes:
✓ Momentum → Describes the quantity of motion of an object and is a vector quantity.

◆ LINEAR MOMENTUM
✓ p = mv

✓ Unit → kg·m/s.

✓ Momentum → Has the same direction as velocity.

◆ CHANGE IN MOMENTUM
✓ Δp = pf − pi

✓ For constant mass:
Δp = m(vf − vi)

◆ IMPULSE
✓ Impulse → The change in momentum:
J = Δp

✓ For a constant net force:
J = FΔt

✓ Therefore:
FΔt = Δp

✓ For a varying force → Impulse is the area under the force–time graph.

◆ IMPULSE–MOMENTUM THEOREM
✓ Fnet = Δp/Δt

✓ A given change in momentum → Can be produced by a large force acting briefly or a smaller force acting for a longer time.

◆ SAFETY APPLICATIONS
✓ Airbags, crumple zones and other safety systems → Increase the time over which momentum changes, thereby reducing average impact force.

◆ CONSERVATION OF LINEAR MOMENTUM
✓ For an isolated system with negligible external net force:

Total momentum before = Total momentum after

m₁v₁i + m₂v₂i = m₁v₁f + m₂v₂f

◆ COLLISIONS
✓ Elastic collision → Momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

✓ Inelastic collision → Momentum is conserved, but kinetic energy is not conserved.

✓ Perfectly inelastic collision → Objects stick together after collision and move with a common velocity.

✓ For a perfectly inelastic collision:
m₁v₁i + m₂v₂i = (m₁ + m₂)vf

◆ COLLISIONS IN ONE DIMENSION
✓ Choose a positive direction and assign signs to velocities → Apply conservation of momentum.

✓ For elastic collisions → Both momentum and kinetic energy equations are used.

◆ CENTER OF MASS
✓ Center of mass → The weighted average position of the masses in a system.

✓ For particles along x:
xcm = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂ + ...)/(m₁ + m₂ + ...)

✓ Similarly:
ycm = (m₁y₁ + m₂y₂ + ...)/(m₁ + m₂ + ...)

✓ Motion of the center of mass → Depends on the net external force acting on the system.

◆ CENTER-OF-MASS VELOCITY
✓ vcm = (m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ + ...)/(m₁ + m₂ + ...)

◆ CENTER OF GRAVITY
✓ Center of gravity → The point through which the resultant gravitational force effectively acts.

✓ It can lie outside the physical object.

◆ ROCKET PROPULSION
✓ A rocket accelerates by ejecting gas backward.

✓ Backward momentum of the exhaust → Is accompanied by an equal and opposite change in the rocket's momentum.

✓ Key idea → Momentum is conserved in an isolated system even when kinetic energy is not.
